21: CloudTrail audits control-plane API activity; CloudWatch provides operational metrics, logs, and alarms.
CloudTrail records SageMaker API calls, including model and endpoint deployment actions, so deployment frequency and caller identity can be audited.
AWS Health reports service events and resource-impacting issues; it is not the endpoint utilization and invocation-error telemetry system.
Trusted Advisor provides recommendations, not the detailed deployment audit trail and endpoint error logs required here.
CloudWatch collects endpoint CPU/GPU metrics and container logs, supporting utilization monitoring and investigation of invocation errors.
AWS Config tracks supported resource configurations and compliance, rather than serving as the requested utilization and application-error monitoring service.
22: The historical Kinesis Data Analytics SQL service supported simple streaming transformations of an existing ingestion flow.
Changing ingestion at 20,000 stores introduces widespread deployment work that the existing Firehose integration does not require.
An EMR Spark job can transform the data, but adds cluster and application management for simple transformations.
A fleet of EC2 transformation workers requires provisioning, scaling, retries, and software maintenance.
For the historical service in the exam, SQL streaming transformations reused the existing flow with little code. That legacy SQL service is retired; this is not a current deployment recommendation.
23: Softmax converts multiclass logits into nonnegative values that sum to one.
Dropout randomly disables activations during training to reduce overfitting; it does not create the output probability distribution.
Smooth L1 is a loss function for numeric errors, not a multiclass output normalization function.
Applying softmax to the 10 output logits produces a normalized probability distribution over the 10 animal classes.
ReLU clips negative activations but does not normalize the 10 outputs to sum to one.
24: Residuals retain the direction of prediction error; aggregate squared-error metrics discard that sign.
RMSE squares residuals, so equally large overestimates and underestimates contribute identically.
A residual plot shows positive and negative errors. With residual defined as actual minus predicted, negative residuals indicate overestimation.
AUC evaluates ranking or classification performance and does not reveal the sign of regression errors.
A confusion matrix summarizes discrete classification outcomes, not continuous target overestimation and underestimation.
25: Recall depends on fitted decision boundaries and classification thresholds, not only a scatter plot of the features.
A decision tree can approximate nonlinear regions, but its depth, fitting, and threshold affect recall. The plot cannot establish that it wins.
A linear SVM cannot closely trace the circular class boundary, but its threshold can change recall. No recall ranking follows from the plot alone.
A Gaussian Naive Bayes model might exploit differing feature variances, but its fitted distributions and threshold are unspecified. Highest recall is not guaranteed.
A single perceptron has a linear boundary in these features. Its recall still depends on fitting and threshold, so the figure cannot establish a unique answer.
26: Hyperparameter search ranges can be narrowed by examining how each hyperparameter relates to the objective metric.
The shape of one input feature does not show which maximum-depth values produce good AUC during tuning.
t-SNE visualizes feature-space structure, not the relationship between a tuning parameter and trial quality.
An objective-versus-iteration plot shows training progress, but does not directly identify the useful range of maximum tree depth.
Plotting AUC against maximum tree depth identifies depth ranges with strong performance, helping eliminate expensive or unproductive trials.
27: Repeatable token normalization reduces inconsistent vocabulary representations before word-embedding training.
Keeping only verbs and nouns discards much of the context that a word-embedding model learns from; it is not a required preparation step.
Lowercasing merges capitalization variants such as BROWN and brown into the same vocabulary item when case is not informative.
A fixed stopword dictionary provides a repeatable filtering rule. Its use should still depend on whether those words matter to the downstream task.
Fixing this one typo manually does not define a repeatable operation over a million sentences. A validated automated spelling policy could be useful, but is not specified.
Word2Vec learns dense vectors from tokens and context. Explicit one-hot vectors are not the requested text-cleaning step.
Tokenization converts each sentence into the word units needed to build the vocabulary and context windows for Word2Vec.
28: A Polly pronunciation lexicon defines reusable pronunciations or substitutions for specific words and acronyms.
SSML can fix individual documents, but editing current documents does not create a reusable acronym pronunciation resource for future input.
A pronunciation lexicon applies consistent acronym handling whenever it is selected during synthesis, avoiding repeated edits to future documents.
Speech marks describe timing and alignment in synthesized speech; they do not specify how an acronym should be pronounced.
Amazon Lex builds conversational interfaces and is not the pronunciation customization mechanism for Polly.
29: A widening training–test performance gap indicates overfitting; increase data diversity or regularize the model.
Vanishing gradients are an optimization problem, not a technique to add for better generalization.
Appropriate image augmentation exposes the model to varied views and conditions, reducing dependence on the controlled training setup.
Increasing model complexity can make memorization easier and worsen the existing generalization gap.
Gradient checking validates derivative calculations; it does not directly regularize a correctly implemented model.
L2 penalizes large weights, limiting overly complex fits and helping the model generalize to unseen driver images.
30: CreateTrainingJob requires execution, compute, and output settings; algorithm-specific input requirements make the requested three-answer key incomplete.
Built-in supervised training normally needs a training-data channel. This is one plausible requirement, contributing to the ambiguity of selecting only three.
A validation channel is optional for many algorithms and jobs; it is not a universal requirement.
RoleArn supplies the execution role assumed by SageMaker. It is a required training-job API parameter.
Hyperparameter requirements vary by algorithm, and the API represents them as a string map, not the universal JSON array described here.
A training job needs ResourceConfig, including the instance type and count. This is another required setting beyond the proposed three-answer limit.
OutputDataConfig specifies the model artifact output location. Together with input, role, and compute settings, it makes the question's fixed count problematic.
31: Columnar storage reduces bytes scanned when analytical queries read only a subset of columns.
CSV is row-oriented text, so Athena generally reads and parses more data than with a suitable columnar format.
Parquet stores columns separately and supports compression and metadata-based pruning, reducing I/O for Athena analytical queries.
Compression shrinks JSON but does not give it Parquet's columnar access and pruning advantages.
RecordIO is a record-oriented training format, not the appropriate columnar storage format for Athena SQL analytics.
32: One-hot encoding represents each category with a separate binary indicator column.
Threshold binarization converts numeric values into two states; it does not separately represent all weekday categories.
Create one indicator for each weekday, setting that day's value to 1 and the others to 0.
Tokenization splits text into units; it does not generate the requested binary categorical feature columns.
Normalization rescales numeric features and does not encode distinct weekday categories as binary indicators.
33: Extreme class imbalance can produce high accuracy even when the model misses nearly every positive example.
Deeper trees add capacity but do not correct the minority class's tiny contribution to training and may increase overfitting.
Copying test data into training causes leakage and destroys the validity of the held-out evaluation.
Oversampling the positive class increases its training representation; any added noise must preserve valid feature values and avoid contaminating the test set.
Increasing the false-negative penalty makes missed future paying users more costly, encouraging the model to learn the rare positive class.
Penalizing false positives more strongly encourages conservative positive predictions, usually worsening the failure to detect the minority class.
34: Invalid placeholder values should be treated as missing data and imputed using valid training observations.
Dropping 450 otherwise useful records discards more than 11% of the dataset and is unnecessary when only age is invalid.
Replace zero ages with a mean or median calculated from valid ages in the training split, preserving the other useful information in those records.
Age is relevant because the disease worsens with age; removing the entire feature loses signal from all 4,000 patients.
k-means is a clustering algorithm, not a complete missing-value treatment by itself; it also requires a suitable numeric representation to run.
35: S3 provides scalable dataset storage, while Athena supplies SQL access over cataloged files.
An S3 data lake accommodates many datasets without managing database capacity; Glue metadata and Athena make those files queryable with SQL.
EBS is attached block storage with provisioned capacity and an EC2 dependency, adding management and scaling work.
A provisioned Redshift cluster adds warehouse capacity and loading management when the requirement is a flexible, inexpensive dataset repository.
DynamoDB global tables target replicated key-value access; they are not the natural storage layer for arbitrary analytical training datasets.
36: A model trained on stale observations can lose relevance as products and user behavior change.
A performance decline does not establish that the architecture must be replaced; stale training data should be investigated first.
Changing hyperparameters without incorporating new observations does not teach the model about new products or preferences.
Retraining only on the original dataset preserves the same stale information, even if regularization changes.
Adding recent interactions and inventory data allows retraining to reflect current behavior, followed by validation before deploying the updated model.
37: A data lake separates cataloging, streaming ingestion, analytics, and recommendation model computation.
In the historical architecture, Glue supplies catalog metadata, Kinesis processes live events, Firehose delivers to Elasticsearch, and EMR runs recommendation workloads.
Athena is a query engine rather than the catalog itself, and Glue alone is not the stated personalized recommendation engine.
Kinesis streaming analytics addresses incoming data; assigning it the role of querying historical S3 datasets misplaces that responsibility.
Athena is not the catalog, DynamoDB Streams captures DynamoDB table changes, and Glue does not by itself produce the proposed recommendations.
38: SageMaker framework scripts and custom containers allow an architecture that differs from a fixed built-in algorithm.
The built-in algorithm's supported architecture cannot simply be replaced with Inception through its normal configuration.
An AWS Support request does not make a customer's chosen architecture the built-in service default.
A compatible custom TensorFlow container can package and train the required Inception architecture on SageMaker.
A TensorFlow Estimator can run a custom training script that constructs or loads Inception, avoiding the built-in ResNet restriction.
Installing code on a separate EC2 machine does not turn that instance into a SageMaker managed notebook or configure a managed Inception training job.
39: High training accuracy with much lower test accuracy indicates that the model is not generalizing well.
Increasing the learning rate targets optimization behavior, not the demonstrated overfitting gap, and can make training unstable.
More dropout randomly removes activations during training, discouraging co-adaptation and providing regularization against memorization.
Increasing the dense layer's size adds parameters and can worsen overfitting when training accuracy is already very high.
Training for more epochs can further memorize the training set; it does not directly resolve poor test performance.
40: Audit logging and model-quality alerting require separate telemetry and notification mechanisms.
CloudTrail already captures SageMaker API activity, so implementing a Lambda-based audit logger adds unnecessary code.
CloudTrail supplies the API audit trail; a custom overfitting metric, CloudWatch alarm, and SNS notification provide the requested training alert.
A Lambda function is unnecessary for recording supported SageMaker API events in CloudTrail and adds steps without improving this workflow.
SNS can deliver a message, but it does not detect overfitting by itself. This option omits the metric and alarm or equivalent detection logic.
